Britain's most reliable cars (plus the ones that'll let you down)

We asked 30,000 drivers what their car is really like to own. Here are the most reliable cars you can buy

The financial pressures of the cost-of-living crisis are showing no signs of letting up, with 56% of people in the UK reporting an increase in their outgoings in July compared with the previous month, according to the latest Government data.

advertisment
scroll for more

Worryingly, the cost of fixing faulty cars appears to be rising, too. Data from the latest What Car? Reliability Survey shows that only 81% of issues on cars up to five years old were fixed for free – a figure that's 14% worse than last year. In addition, 12% of issues cost owners up to £500 to repair in the latest survey, compared with just 4% last year, while the number of problems that cost in excess of £1500 to put right has more than doubled from 1.4% to 3%.

These figures show that it’s more important than ever to choose a dependable car. This year’s What Car? Reliability Survey, conducted in association with MotorEasy, provides an insight into 225 models from 30 brands, reporting on the experiences of 39,332 owners over the past two years.

Claire Evans
Updated: 30 September 2026

Much more than a satisfaction poll, it asks owners in detail about the number and nature of any faults, how much they cost to put right and how long it took to rectify them. The two latter factors are the main headaches when your car goes wrong, so we use them to create a unique reliability rating for each brand and model.

Britain's most reliable cars

=1. Mini Countryman (2024-present)

Reliability rating 100%

Most common faults: none

Average repair cost: £0

Time off road: none

The current iteration of the Countryman is larger and roomier than the previous model, and that fact has propelled it from the small SUV sector into the competitive and crowded family SUV class. That’s been no barrier to success here, though, because the Countryman is one of just two models in the 2026 survey to gain a perfect rating of 100%, making it the highest scorer of all 61 models in this class. This means every owner who reported on their car said it had suffered no faults at all.

While it may not have the plushest interior and some may find its driving position awkward, there’s no doubting its credentials if you’re after the most dependable family SUV.

Owner's comment: "It’s the best car I’ve ever had. It has been simply faultless in terms of reliability."

“The family SUV of the modern Mini range, the Countryman doesn’t seem as naturally suited to driver entertainment as its lower, lighter Mini Cooper hatchback stablemate, but it does just as much to put you in the mood when you get behind the wheel. And it's reassuring to know that the model ranks highly for reliability, thanks to its robust, BMW-sourced mechanical foundations.”  – Chris Haining, Sub Editor

The Swift’s flawless performance played a big part in propelling Suzuki back to the top of the brand league table for the first time since 2018.

3. Toyota Aygo X (2021-present)

Reliability rating 99.7%

Most common faults: bodywork 3%

The Aygo X is remarkably consistent when it comes to dependability. It was the second-highest-scoring small car in last year’s survey, with precisely the same score as it gained this year.

Toyota’s smallest model out-ranks the Yaris, which ranks 13th in the same category, with a fault rate of 20%, whereas a mere 3% of the Aygo Xs we were told about suffered a problem.

The only area that gave owners any concern was the bodywork, and all of the affected cars could still be driven. Toyota sorted out all of the issues for free, and all work was completed in a day or less.

Owner’s comment: “The thing I like the most about my Aygo X is that it has not let me down once in three years' of driving.”

No owners were left out of pocket, either; even though some of the affected cars would have been outside BMW’s new car warranty period.

5. Mini hatchback (2014-2024)

Most common faults: non-engine electrics 2%, steering 2%

In spite of its advancing years, the now-discontinued Mini hatchback looks more robust than its replacement, the Mini Cooper. Its reliability rating is a full 10% higher than the newer model’s, and it has experienced far fewer faults; just 4% of Mini hatchbacks went wrong, compared with 24% of Coopers.

Non-engine electrical issues and problems relating to the steering were the main gripes of the owners who reported a fault. All of the problematic cars could still be driven, and they were all fixed for free. It’s just a shame they were all out of action for more than a week.

Lexus has recently introduced an all-new electric ES, but that doesn’t mean you should disregard its combustion-engined predecessor. The seventh-generation ES is a comfortable and efficient saloon with hybrid technology that helps it to reduce running costs.

Its other big plus point is near-faultless dependability. Just 6% of the ESs we heard about had any problems, and the only area to give any grief was the infotainment system. Unlike the electrical glitches suffered by the Mercedes C-Class, which contributed to that model’s lengthy stints in the workshop, the issues that affected ESs were all resolved in a day or less. Porsche's smallest SUV is designed to appeal to keen drivers who need more practicality than they’d find in a sports car. As well as being great fun to drive, the combustion-powered Macan is pretty bulletproof.

Bodywork was the most frequently cited problem area, followed by the Macan’s gearbox and non-engine electrics. Overall, 13% of the Q2s in our survey had a defect, caused by the brakes, the engine and its electrics, the fuel system and a range of non-engine electrical issues. None of these glitches stopped any cars from being driven, and all of the affected vehicles were in and out of the workshop on the same day, causing a minimum of disruption for owners. The Fabia is an excellent value small hatchback that's fitted with a range of efficient engines and adheres to Skoda's Simply Clever philosophy, which aims to provide clever features to solve simple problems, such as having an umbrella tucked away in the driver's door. Although 12% of the Fabias in our survey went wrong, all cars could still be driven, and the most common complaint was about minor interior trim flaws. No surprise, then, that half of the cars with faults were fixed in a day or less. Best of all Skoda paid for all remedial work.

The 10 most unreliable cars

Here are the cars that have the highest percentage of owner-reported problems in our survey — and the ones which could be most deserving of breakdown cover.

1. Volkswagen Tiguan (2024-present)

Reliability rating 55.3%

Most common faults: non-engine electrics 50%, sat-nav/infotainment system 30%, bodywork 20%, brakes 15%, 12-volt battery 10%, engine electrics 10%, gearbox 10%, interior trim 10%

Average repair cost: 90% fixed for free, 10% £1-£100

Time off road: 44% more than a week, 30% one day to a week

The Tiguan was the lowest-scoring model in last year’s survey, and things haven’t improved for Volkswagen’s conventionally powered family SUV. Not only is it the lowest ranked model in this class, but it also takes the wooden spoon as the poorest scorer overall.

advertisment
scroll for more

A staggering 75% of the cars we were told about had some kind of failure, half of which concerned non-engine electrics. Owners also cited the 12-volt battery, bodywork, brakes, engine electrics and infotainment as problematic. While 27% of issues were put right in a day or less, 44% took more than a week to resolve. Better news is that Volkswagen paid for 90% of repairs, and no owners paid more than £100 per fault.

Owner’s view: “My Tiguan has suffered a constant stream of issues, and some took far too long to get fixed.”

How the research was carried out

The What Car? Reliability Survey, conducted in association with MotorEasy, is open to everyone who visits whatcar.com or subscribes to What Car? magazine. Responses were received from car owners around the UK.

We ask them to tell us if their car had suffered a fault in the previous 24 months, and if so what area of the car was affected. We then ask them to expand on this by telling us how much they had to pay to get the fault fixed and how long their car was in the workshop.

advertisment
scroll for more

We use the information to create a unique reliability rating for each model and brand where we have a large enough response rate. These two factors are more important than how many faults a car suffered, because they determine how much inconvenience and expense a problem caused.

To gain an in-depth understanding of what goes wrong, we asked owners to describe issues in 16 categories: 12-volt battery, air-con/cooling system, EV battery (electric vehicles and hybrids), bodywork, brakes, engine/electric motor, engine or motor electrics, exhaust, fuel/charging system, gearbox/clutch, interior trim, non-engine or motor electrics, sat-nav/infotainment, steering, suspension and other.

The minimum sample size at brand level is 70 responses, and at model level it is 15. While models with fewer than 15 responses are not reported on, all the responses are used to create the brand rating. 

Are cars getting more reliable?

We've seen an improvement in reliability over the past seven years – the percentage of cars aged up to five years old going wrong has dropped from 27% in 2018 to 23% in 2026.

advertisment
scroll for more

However, the percentage of cars being fixed for free by manufacturers has fallen significantly - it was 95% last year and only 81% this time round. 

The cost of fixing the most expensive faults has risen, too. Three percent of repair bills totalled more than £1500 this year - that's more than double the 1.4% that cost this amount last year. 

What are the most reliable cars and brands?

After seven years of being a bridesmaid, Suzuki has returned to the top of our league table. Its rating signifies that almost all of the cars its owners told us about have an exemplary reliability record. The best of them was the previous-generation Swift, one of only two models to gain a perfect score this year, while the Vitara wasn’t far behind.

Honda and Mini, in second and third places respectively, are both previous winners and still look like extremely strong choices for anyone who is after a car that won’t let them down. Four Honda models scored 95% or more: the current Civic, HR-V, Jazz and ZR-V. The current Mini Countryman was the second model to achieve a 100% rating, and the 2014-2024 Mini hatchback was just behind it (99.4%).

advertisment
scroll for more

Normally dependable Lexus and Toyota are out of the top 10 this year, because many of their models have suffered battery problems. BMW has sunk down, too, due to a combination of slow repairs, lots of electrical issues and some costly bills.

The brand that has improved the most is MG, which has implemented big changes to improve wait times and the cost of repairs for its customers. 

There are a couple of VW Group brands near the bottom of the chart, dragged down mainly by electrical issues that have been slow and sometimes costly to sort out. Volkswagen’s score was dented by ongoing issues with the Tiguan, the lowest-scoring model in the survey, while Audi was hit by the performances of the current A3 and previous-generation Q5.

That leaves Land Rover as the least reliable brand in this year’s survey. Although the Range Rover Sport and Range Rover scored well, this was offset by very poor performances by the Discovery Sport and Evoque. We’d advise you to choose carefully if you want a dependable Land Rover.

advertisment
scroll for more

Are petrol, diesel, electric or hybrid cars most reliable?

Despite the growing popularity of electric vehicles, it’s a petrol model you should go for if you want a car that’s least likely to develop a fault and leave you stranded at the roadside.

Our data shows that only 20% of petrol models were afflicted by faults. In contrast, 32% of diesel models let their owners down, making them the least dependable fuel type. Electric models weren’t far ahead of diesels for the frequency of faults, because 27% went wrong, while hybrids looked more promising with a 23% fault rate.

Petrol cars were also the least likely to spend a long time off the road; 34% of those that went wrong were fixed in a day or less and 39% took more than a week to rectify.

Diesel models spent only a little longer in the workshop on average – 40% were out of action for more than seven days – but they were the least likely to be fixed for free. Car makers took care of bills for 74% of diesel car owners, compared with 88% for electric cars. However, the latter took the longest to fix on average, with 47% of those that went wrong out of action for more than a week.

advertisment
scroll for more

How MG fixed its reliability woes

MG is the most-improved brand in this year’s survey, jumping from last place in 2025 to ninth overall. The improvement is the result of a number of significant changes in the way it supplies parts, fixes cars and looks after customers.

A key part of the improvement has been the investment in a huge new parts warehouse and distribution centre in partnership with XPO Logistics. This was opened in November 2025, and it provides overnight delivery to dealerships for 96% of necessary parts, with arrival before 8am.

The Northamptonshire site holds more than 10,000 different components and operates from 6am to 10pm, delivering 2500 parts every day. It takes in eight container loads of parts each day from China; these are quality checked and stacked in specific locations on the shelves via a computer-controlled system.

Meanwhile, MG has worked on improving the way faults are fixed by adopting a ‘triage’ system in technical support. First and second-tier technicians work on troublesome cars for the first three weeks, but after that a specialist ‘flying doctor’, who is the most highly trained engineer, will literally be flown in to help.

advertisment
scroll for more

Training has been expanded across all areas of the company, with more than 2000 members of staff completing courses at MG’s UK training centre last year. There’s more monitoring and mystery shopping of dealerships than before, so that any that aren’t up to scratch can be helped to improve. A Technician of the Year award has also been introduced, alongside a £3 million scheme that rewards employees for excellent behaviour.

Finally, to ensure customers aren’t inconvenienced if their cars go wrong, the car maker has invested in a fleet of courtesy cars, so owners can have a like-for-like vehicle until their own is back on the road without having to rely on the dealer to supply this.

About the report author

Claire Evans has been a motoring journalist for more than 30 years, much of that time spent specialising in consumer issues. She was a troubleshooting advice columnist for Carweek magazine in the 1990s, helping car owners with faulty cars get the right level of reparation from car makers.

She also spent six years working on motoring content for Which?, and it is here she oversaw the running of the charity's annual used car reliability survey.

Claire launched the What Car? Reliability Survey in 2017, and since then has helped thousands of buyers choose the most reliable new cars and SUVs, as well as the most dependable used cars. The survey data is also shared with car makers, who use it to find out more about issues with models and the areas where they could provide better customer service.
